task1.title: Salisbury College course trends
task1.prompt: The charts below show the percentage of students following different types of course at Salisbury College in 1984, 1994 and 2004.

chartDesc.overview: Between 1984 and 2004, the proportion of students enrolled in face-to-face courses decreased, while online courses grew significantly following their introduction by 1994.
unreadable: Percentage values for Mixed-media course and Correspondence course in 1984 visual are omitted in the original image.
Percentage values for Mixed-media course and Correspondence course in 1994 visual are omitted in the original image.
Percentage values for Correspondence courses, Mixed-media course, and Face-to-face courses in 2004 visual are omitted in the original image.
keyFeatures: In 1984 (Students by course type 1984), Face-to-face courses held the largest share at 67%.
In 1994 (Students by course type 1994), Face-to-face courses declined to 53%, while On-line courses were at 12%.
In 2004 (Students by course type 2004), On-line courses increased to 35%.

task1.instruction: Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparison where relevant.
task1.sampleBand5:
The pie charts show the different types of courses at Salisbury College in three different years. They show the percentage of students in 1984, 1994, and 2004.

In 1984, most students did vocational courses, which was 58%. Academic courses were the second most popular, with 32%. Art and design was the least popular at only 10%. In 1994, the percentage of students doing vocational courses went down to 40%. Academic courses increased to 45%, becoming the most popular. Art and design also increased slightly to 15%.

In 2004, there were more changes. Vocational courses decreased again to 35%. Academic courses stayed about the same at 46%. However, art and design increased a lot, to 19%. So, over time, vocational courses became less popular and art and design became more popular, but academic courses stayed quite similar.
task1.sampleBand6:
The pie charts give information about the proportion of students at Salisbury College studying different courses in 1984, 1994 and 2004.

Overall, the percentage of students taking vocational courses saw the biggest change, while the proportion of students doing science courses remained fairly stable. Arts courses also saw a decrease over the period.

In 1984, vocational courses accounted for 30% of students, which was the smallest proportion. Science courses were the most popular, with 40%, and arts courses accounted for the remaining 30%. By 1994, the percentage of students taking vocational courses had increased to 35%, slightly exceeding the proportion of students taking arts courses which had fallen to 25%. Science courses remained the most popular, but had decreased to 40%.

In 2004, there was a significant increase in students taking vocational courses, rising to 45%. This made vocational courses the most popular. Science courses remained stable at 30%, while the percentage of arts students saw a further decrease to 25%. It is clear that vocational courses became much more popular over the 20 year period.
task1.sampleBand7:
The pie charts illustrate the proportion of students at Salisbury College enrolled in different courses across three distinct years: 1984, 1994, and 2004.

Overall, the most striking feature is the significant decline in students undertaking vocational courses, while the proportion pursuing humanities subjects experienced a marked increase. Science courses remained relatively stable throughout the period.

In 1984, vocational courses accounted for the largest share, with 40% of students enrolled. Humanities and science courses represented 30% each. A decade later, in 1994, the percentage of vocational students had decreased to 32%, while humanities had risen to 35%. Science courses remained at 33%, demonstrating a degree of consistency.

By 2004, the trend had become even more pronounced. The proportion of students studying humanities reached a peak of 45%, surpassing all other course types. Vocational courses had dropped further to 25%, indicating a substantial shift in student preferences. Science courses experienced a slight decrease to 30%, continuing their stable but declining trend.
task1.sampleBand8:
The pie charts illustrate the proportion of students at Salisbury College enrolled in various course types across three distinct years: 1984, 1994, and 2004.

Overall, the data reveals a noticeable shift away from vocational courses towards degree programs, with a corresponding fluctuation in the popularity of language courses. Short courses remained the least favoured option throughout the entire period.

In 1984, vocational courses were the most prevalent, accounting for 40% of student enrolment. Degree courses represented 35%, while language courses comprised 20%. Short courses were the least popular, with only 5% of students participating. By 1994, the percentage of students undertaking degree courses had risen significantly to 45%, overtaking vocational courses, which decreased to 30%. Language courses experienced a slight increase to 23%, while short courses remained at 2%.

The trend towards degree courses became even more pronounced by 2004. Degree courses accounted for half of all students (50%), while vocational courses continued their decline to 25%. Language courses experienced a dip to 20%, and short courses maintained their position as the least popular option, falling to just 5%. It is evident that degree courses gained traction over the period, at the expense of vocational studies.
task1.sampleBand9:
The pie charts illustrate the distribution of students across various course types at Salisbury College in 1984, 1994, and 2004.

Overall, vocational courses represented the largest proportion of students throughout the period. While the percentage of students enrolled in language courses experienced a noticeable decline, the proportion undertaking science courses saw a corresponding increase.

In 1984, vocational courses accounted for 50% of the student population, dwarfing the other categories. Language courses were the second most popular, attracting 30% of students, followed by science and other courses, each with 10%. Ten years later, in 1994, the dominance of vocational courses was further cemented, increasing to 60%. By 2004, the trend of vocational courses being the most popular continued, with their share reaching a peak of 65%. The proportion of science students increased again, accounting for 20% of the student body. In contrast, language courses experienced a further contraction, falling to just 5%. The remaining 10% were enrolled in other courses. These figures reveal a clear shift in focus over the two decades, from language to science and, overwhelmingly, to vocational training. The fluctuations in popularity underscore the evolving educational landscape at Salisbury College. A discernible pattern emerges showing the rising prominence of vocational studies. The data offers a compelling snapshot of changing student priorities. The most striking feature is the consistent growth in vocational course enrollment.
task1.sampleAnswer:
The pie charts illustrate how the distribution of students across different course types at Salisbury College changed over a twenty-year period from 1984 to 2004. Overall, there was a significant shift away from traditional academic courses toward vocational and skills-based programs.

In 1984, academic courses dominated student enrollment, accounting for approximately 50% of all students. Vocational courses represented about 30%, while the remaining 20% was split between language courses and skills training programs.

By 1994, the picture had begun to change. Academic courses had declined to around 40% of total enrollment, while vocational courses increased to approximately 35%. Language courses remained stable at about 10%, and skills training grew slightly to 15%.

The most dramatic changes occurred by 2004. Vocational courses had become the most popular option, representing roughly 45% of students. Academic courses had fallen further to just 30%. Skills training courses also saw substantial growth, reaching about 18%, while language courses remained relatively steady at approximately 7%.

This trend suggests a growing emphasis on practical, job-oriented education over traditional academic study.

Fan kurslari 30% da barqaror bo'lib qoldi, san'at talabalari foizi esa yana yanada kamayishni ko'rdi va 25% ga tushdi. Ma'lumki, kasbiy kurslar 20 yil ichida ancha ommabop bo'lib ketdi.

task2.title: Annual driving tests
task2.prompt: The best way to make roads safer is to make vehicle drivers take a driving test each year. To what extent do you agree or disagree?
task2.instruction: To what extent do you agree or disagree?
task2.sampleBand5:
Many people think that the best way to improve road safety is to make all drivers take a driving test every year. I partly agree with this idea, but I also think there are other things that can help.

One reason why yearly tests could be good is because it helps to make sure people still know the rules. Some drivers might forget things over time, especially if they have been driving for many years. A test could remind them about important safety things, like speed limits and what to do at junctions. This could possibly make them drive better.

However, just testing drivers might not be enough. Some people are bad drivers even if they know the rules. Also, tests can be expensive and take a lot of time. It would be a big job to test everyone every year, and it might not be practical. Other things are also important, like making sure roads are well-maintained and that cars are safe.

Another thing is about new technology. Cars are getting smarter, with things like automatic braking and lane assist. These things can help drivers avoid accidents. The government should invest more in these technologies and encourage people to use them. Also, better education about road safety for all people, not just drivers, could make a big difference. This means teaching children about crossing the road safely and making sure everyone understands the dangers of things like drinking and driving. In conclusion, while testing drivers every year could help, it is not the only answer. A combination of things, like better technology, education, and road maintenance, is needed to make roads safer for everyone.
task2.sampleBand6:
Many people believe that the most effective way to improve road safety is to require drivers to retake their driving test every year. While I agree that regular testing can play a role, I don't think it is the best or only solution. I believe a combination of factors, including driver education and better road infrastructure, are also important.

On the one hand, yearly driving tests could potentially identify drivers who have developed bad habits or whose skills have deteriorated. This is especially true for older drivers, whose reaction times may have slowed down. By requiring regular testing, these drivers could be identified and either given remedial training or, in extreme cases, have their licenses revoked. This could help to reduce the number of accidents caused by incompetent drivers. However, this approach may not be practical due to the cost and logistical challenges of testing all drivers annually.

On the other hand, focusing solely on testing neglects other important aspects of road safety. For instance, improved driver education, especially for new drivers, could instill safer driving habits from the outset. Furthermore, investing in better road infrastructure, such as clearer road markings, improved signage, and safer road design, could also significantly reduce accidents. In addition, stricter enforcement of existing traffic laws, such as speeding and drunk driving, could also contribute to safer roads. These measures address the root causes of many accidents, rather than just identifying drivers who may already be a risk.

In conclusion, while annual driving tests may have some benefits, I believe that a more comprehensive approach is needed to make roads safer. This should include improved driver education, better road infrastructure, and stricter law enforcement. Relying solely on testing is unlikely to be the most effective solution in the long run.
task2.sampleBand7:
The proposition that annual driving tests are the optimal method for enhancing road safety is, in my opinion, an oversimplification. While regular testing could potentially identify and remediate deficiencies in driving skills, I believe a more multifaceted approach is necessary to effectively address this complex issue.

On the one hand, the implementation of yearly driving tests could lead to several benefits. For instance, such tests would likely identify drivers who have developed bad habits over time, or whose skills have deteriorated due to age or health issues. This would allow for targeted retraining or, in extreme cases, the removal of dangerous drivers from the road. Furthermore, the mere prospect of a yearly test could encourage drivers to be more conscious of their driving habits and to adhere more strictly to traffic laws. This could lead to a general improvement in driving standards and a reduction in accidents.

However, focusing solely on annual testing overlooks other critical factors that contribute to road safety. Road design and maintenance, for example, play a significant role. Poorly designed intersections, inadequate lighting, and poorly maintained road surfaces can all contribute to accidents, regardless of the skill of the driver. Moreover, vehicle safety standards are also paramount. Modern vehicles are equipped with numerous safety features, such as anti-lock brakes and airbags, which significantly reduce the risk of serious injury in the event of a collision. Therefore, investing in improved road infrastructure and promoting the use of safer vehicles are equally important considerations.

In addition, the effectiveness of annual testing could be undermined by practical challenges. The logistical difficulties and costs associated with testing all drivers every year would be considerable. Furthermore, a test conducted on a single day may not accurately reflect a driver's typical driving behavior. A driver who performs well on the test might still engage in risky behavior at other times. Therefore, while annual testing may have some merit, it is not a panacea for road safety problems.

In conclusion, while I acknowledge that annual driving tests could contribute to improved road safety by identifying and addressing deficiencies in driving skills, I believe that a more comprehensive strategy is required. This strategy should encompass improvements to road infrastructure, stricter vehicle safety standards, and ongoing driver education, rather than relying solely on yearly testing. This holistic approach offers a more sustainable and effective solution to the challenge of making our roads safer for everyone.
task2.sampleBand8:
The proposition that annual driving tests are the optimal solution for enhancing road safety is a contentious one. While regular evaluations could potentially address driver competency, I believe that a more multifaceted approach, incorporating technological advancements and targeted educational campaigns, would yield more significant and sustainable improvements.

Undeniably, mandatory yearly testing has some merit. It would ensure that drivers maintain a certain level of proficiency and remain conversant with updated traffic regulations. For instance, drivers might become complacent over time, forgetting crucial aspects of road safety or developing bad habits. A regular test could rectify these issues, potentially reducing accidents caused by driver error. Furthermore, such a system could weed out individuals whose driving skills have deteriorated due to age or medical conditions, thereby safeguarding vulnerable road users.

However, focusing solely on annual testing overlooks other crucial factors contributing to road accidents. The relentless pursuit of technological innovation in vehicles, such as advanced driver-assistance systems (ADAS) including automatic emergency braking and lane departure warning, offers a more proactive and arguably more effective approach. These systems can mitigate the impact of human error and even prevent accidents from occurring in the first place. Moreover, targeted public awareness campaigns addressing specific issues such as distracted driving and speeding can foster a culture of responsible road use. These campaigns, when coupled with stricter enforcement of existing traffic laws, can prove to be immensely beneficial.

In conclusion, while annual driving tests may contribute to safer roads by ensuring driver competence, they represent only one piece of a much larger puzzle. A more holistic strategy, leveraging technological advancements and prioritizing public education alongside robust enforcement, is more likely to yield a substantial and lasting impact on road safety. It is through this comprehensive approach, rather than a singular focus on testing, that we can truly create safer roads for all. To solely rely on annual testing would be to neglect the significant potential of other, perhaps more impactful, interventions. Such a narrow focus would, ultimately, be a disservice to public safety. Therefore, I respectfully disagree with the proposal.
task2.sampleBand9:
The proposition that annual driving tests constitute the optimal strategy for enhancing road safety is, in my estimation, an oversimplification. While periodic assessments undoubtedly possess merit, they represent only one facet of a multifaceted issue demanding a more holistic and comprehensive approach. I contend that, while potentially beneficial, mandatory yearly re-testing is neither the most effective nor the most economically viable solution.

Undeniably, requiring drivers to retake their tests annually could serve as a powerful deterrent against negligent driving habits. Such regular evaluations would, theoretically, ensure that drivers remain conversant with current traffic regulations and maintain a requisite level of competence behind the wheel. This is especially pertinent given the constant evolution of road infrastructure and traffic management systems. However, the practical implications of implementing such a policy are considerable. The logistical burden on testing facilities would be immense, potentially leading to protracted waiting times and increased costs for both individuals and the government. Furthermore, the inherent stress associated with testing could lead to anxiety-induced errors, skewing the results and failing to accurately reflect a driver's typical performance.

Conversely, a more targeted approach, focusing on high-risk drivers or those with a history of traffic violations, would likely yield more substantial results. Implementing stricter penalties for traffic offenses, coupled with mandatory remedial training for repeat offenders, could prove far more effective in curbing dangerous driving behaviour. Moreover, investing in public awareness campaigns aimed at promoting responsible driving habits and fostering a culture of road safety could have a far-reaching impact. Technological advancements, such as the integration of advanced driver-assistance systems (ADAS) in vehicles and the deployment of intelligent traffic management systems, also hold significant promise in mitigating accidents and improving overall road safety. These strategies address the root causes of accidents, rather than simply testing drivers' knowledge.

In conclusion, while the notion of annual driving tests might appear, at first glance, to be a straightforward solution to improve road safety, a more nuanced perspective reveals its limitations. A combination of targeted interventions, stricter enforcement of existing regulations, public awareness campaigns, and the judicious application of technology offers a more sustainable and cost-effective path towards achieving safer roads for all. To rely solely on annual testing would be to ignore the myriad of other factors that contribute to road accidents and to neglect more promising avenues for improvement. The issue is far more complex and requires a multi-pronged strategy to be truly effective. Therefore, I disagree with the proposition.
task2.sampleAnswer:
Some people argue that requiring drivers to pass an annual driving test would significantly improve road safety. While I acknowledge that regular assessment could have some benefits, I largely disagree that this approach represents the best solution to making roads safer.

Proponents of yearly driving tests contend that they would ensure drivers maintain their skills and knowledge of traffic laws over time. Such tests could identify those whose abilities have diminished due to age, health issues, or simply bad habits developed since their original test. Knowing that an annual assessment is approaching might also encourage drivers to stay more vigilant and maintain safer driving practices throughout the year.

However, there are several compelling reasons why this proposal is problematic. Firstly, the administrative and financial burden would be enormous. Testing millions of drivers annually would require significant government resources and create considerable inconvenience for citizens. Secondly, passing a driving test does not necessarily guarantee safe driving in real-world conditions; many accidents are caused by momentary lapses in concentration, deliberate risk-taking, or driving under the influence—behaviors that a test cannot prevent.

More effective alternatives exist for improving road safety. These include investing in better road infrastructure, implementing stricter penalties for dangerous driving offenses, enhancing vehicle safety standards, and utilizing technology such as speed cameras and breathalyzer ignition locks. Educational campaigns about the dangers of distracted driving and drink-driving could also yield significant results.

In conclusion, while the idea of annual driving tests has some merit, the practical difficulties and limited effectiveness make it an impractical solution. A combination of infrastructure improvements, stricter enforcement, and public education would be more effective approaches to road safety.

Ko'pchilik yo'l xavfsizligini yaxshilashning eng yaxshi usuli barcha haydovchilarni har yili haydovchilik imtihonidan o'tkazish deb hisoblaydi. Men bu fikrga qisman qo'shilaman, lekin menimcha, yordam beradigan boshqa narsalar ham bor.

Yillik imtihonlar yaxshi bo'lishining bir sababi, bu odamlarning qoidalarni hali ham bilishiga ishonch hosil qilishga yordam beradi. Ba'zi haydovchilar vaqt o'tishi bilan, ayniqsa, ko'p yillar davomida haydashgan bo'lsa, narsalarni unutishi mumkin. Imtihon ularga tezlik chegaralari va chorrahalarda nima qilish kerakligi kabi muhim xavfsizlik narsalarini eslatishi mumkin. Bu ularni ehtimol yaxshiroq haydashga undashi mumkin.

Biroq, faqat haydovchilarni sinovdan o'tkazish kifoya qilmasligi mumkin. Ba'zi odamlar qoidalarni bilishsa ham, yomon haydovchi bo'lishi mumkin. Shuningdek, imtihonlar qimmatga tushishi va ko'p vaqt talab qilishi mumkin. Har bir kishini har yili sinovdan o'tkazish katta ish bo'lar edi va bu amaliy bo'lmasligi mumkin. Yo'llar yaxshi saqlanishi va mashinalar xavfsiz bo'lishi kabi boshqa narsalar ham muhim.

Yana bir narsa - bu yangi texnologiya haqida. Mashinalar avtomatik tormozlash va yo'lakni ushlab turish kabi narsalar bilan aqllashib bormoqda. Bu narsalar haydovchilarga baxtsiz hodisalardan qochishga yordam berishi mumkin. Hukumat bu texnologiyalarga ko'proq sarmoya kiritishi va odamlarni ulardan foydalanishga undashi kerak. Shuningdek, nafaqat haydovchilar, balki barcha odamlar uchun yo'l xavfsizligi bo'yicha yaxshiroq ta'lim katta farq qilishi mumkin. Bu bolalarga yo'lni xavfsiz tarzda kesib o'tishni o'rgatish va hamma ichkilik ichish va haydash kabi xavflarni tushunishini ta'minlashni anglatadi. Xulosa qilib aytganda, haydovchilarni har yili sinovdan o'tkazish yordam berishi mumkin bo'lsa-da, bu yagona javob emas. Yo'llarni hamma uchun xavfsizroq qilish uchun yaxshiroq texnologiya, ta'lim va yo'llarni ta'mirlash kabi narsalar kombinatsiyasi kerak.
task2.uzSampleBand6:
Ko'pchilik odamlar yo'l harakati xavfsizligini yaxshilashning eng samarali yo'li haydovchilardan har yili haydovchilik imtihonini qayta topshirishni talab qilish deb hisoblaydi. Men muntazam test o'tkazish muhim rol o'ynashi mumkinligiga qo'shilaman, lekin bu eng yaxshi yoki yagona yechim deb o'ylamayman.
